outside.why: The reading’s admission, “I know not what profiteth or harmeth me”, is here a soldier’s proverb: we often beg for what would hurt us. Shakespeare’s speaker is consoled by prayers refused; the reading asks that the choice be made for it.
The same pair, the good of this world and of the next, asked for in one breath. The Qur’an gives it as the prayer of those who ask well, just after speaking of those who ask for this world only.

The reading’s words, “Leave me not alone, for Thou art the Best of inheritors”, are Zachariah’s in the Qur’an: an old man asking for a child. The prayer keeps his cry and drops the particular lack, so that any solitude can say it.

The same doubled address, “My God, my God”, from the other side of the fear: the Psalmist has been left, and asks why. Can the reading’s plea not to be forsaken be prayed by someone who already feels that he is?
Moses, sent to face Pharaoh, asks for the two things the reading asks: that the task be made easy and that a knot be loosed. His knot is in his own tongue; the reading’s are in “affairs”.

The fable’s god answers a prayer to be got out of the mire with an order to push. The reading asks God to untie the knots and says there is no other helper. Does asking that the difficult be made easy leave the shoulder at the wheel?

The reading ends by asking that debts be redeemed and needs satisfied. The prayer Jesus taught asks for one day’s bread, and ties the forgiving of debts to forgiving one’s own debtors, a condition the reading does not make.

A prayer the Prophet is reported to have said often names together what these two readings ask relief from: worry and grief, and the weight of debt. It adds failings of one’s own, laziness and cowardice, to the things to be delivered from.

The reading calls on the God who answers the cry of those who cry out. The anchoress Julian, doubting whether her prayers were heard, reports this reply: the asking itself was put there by the one who is asked.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá tells a grieving woman that he prays for her morning and evening. When a disciple asks leave to pray for the sick Confucius, the Master sets the offer aside: his whole life has been his prayer. What does a prayer said for someone add to a life lived well?

The Gāyatrī, the most often recited verse of the Rig Veda, asks the same gift: light for the mind, from Savitar, the sun at its rising. It is said in the plural, “we”, where the reading asks for one lowly person.

The reading asks “a way out” for someone in a strait. The Qur’an promises one, in those words, to whoever keeps faith, with provision from where none was looked for; a later reading asks to be sustained “through means I cannot reckon”.

The reading asks God to light a lamp for a man, and an earlier one calls God the refuge of the frightened. The Buddha, near death, tells his attendant to seek neither lamp nor refuge outside himself. Is a lamp that has been asked for still one’s own?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that a mighty burden be lightened by handing a trust back to God. Jesus invites the heavy laden to the same exchange and says plainly that it is one: rest comes with another yoke, a light one.

The emperor would turn the prayer round: not release from the burden but freedom from needing release. The reading asks for relief, and an earlier one for rescue from anguish. What would be left to ask if the wish itself were changed?

Both pray face down, and both speak of a cup. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that the chalice of martyrdom be given him; Jesus asks that the cup pass, and yields. Which is harder to pray for: the cup, or a will that is not one’s own?

A poet in prison claims the freedom the reading shows in its prisoner, who is “wholly detached” and whose eyes are on something the walls do not shut out. Lovelace finds it in love and a quiet mind; the reading’s prisoner in turning toward mercy.

Johnson ends his poem on the wishes that ruin people with this counsel: go on praying, but leave the measure and the choice to Heaven. Three readings do so: “I know not what will help or harm me”; “ordain for me the best of what lieth with Thee”.

The reading’s sentence, “You know what is within my soul while I know not what is within Your Self”, is spoken in the Qur’an by Jesus, answering God. There it clears him of a charge; in the reading it becomes the ground for asking only what is best.

Paine’s charge against all petition is that it tells God the petitioner knows better. The reading asks only for “that which is best for me” and says who knows what that is. Does Paine’s objection touch a prayer that does not choose?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá says he bows his head in supplication “at every breath”. Sa‘dī opens his Rose Garden by counting what each breath owes: two benefits, in and out, and thanks due for both, which no hand or tongue can pay.

The reading is a blessing said over others: may you be protected, may you be bright each morning. The blessing the Torah gives the priests to say over the people has the same shape: keeping first, then a shining face.

The dying Arthur asks his last knight for what ‘Abdu’l-Bahá gives unasked in three readings: prayer for friends, “night and day”. Tennyson’s king adds a reason: such prayer is what binds the round earth to God.

David’s blessing over the gifts for the temple runs as the Báb’s testimony does: “Thine is…”, said until the list of what belongs to God has no remainder. In both, the one who prays owns nothing on the list.

The Báb’s praise climbs past every praise that created things can offer. Laozi begins where that climb ends: what can be named is not the lasting name. The prayer goes on naming all the same. Is that a contradiction, or the point?

Jesus warns against thinking that many words are what is heard. The Báb’s prayers here are long and repeat one frame dozens of times. Is this the repetition Jesus rejects, or does a litany of praise do something that a request does not?

The reading is a blessing on Muhammad and his family, drawn out through one divine attribute after another. The verse that asks believers for such blessings is two sentences long; the Báb’s prayer is one way of obeying it.

Tagore tells the worshipper to stop chanting and open his eyes: God is out with the tiller and the stone-breaker, in the dust. Three readings here are chant of the highest order. Do they fall under the poet’s rebuke, or belong to another hour than the tiller’s?

The Báb testifies “in this hour of this night”, which God has honoured and magnified. The Qur’an speaks so of one night, that of its own revelation, better than a thousand months; the reading gives its hour the same kind of honour.

The reading asks that a smouldering love be set aglow. Wesley’s journal records such a moment in plain words and to the quarter hour: his heart “strangely warmed”. It came, he says, at a meeting he had gone to unwillingly.

A priest’s sonnet makes the reading’s plea in the reading’s season: everything is in leaf, the birds build, and he asks not to be the one thing left dry. Hopkins lets his complaint stand beside the request; the reading keeps to the asking.

The reading’s leaf waits for the breeze of mercy to pass over it and move it. Shelley asks as much of the autumn wind: to be its lyre, his dead thoughts driven like leaves toward a new birth. His wind has no mercy to appeal to. What is being asked when one asks only to be moved?

Two readings ask to be quickened by the breath of the Holy Spirit; one says outright, “We are dead; quicken us.” Ezekiel is shown the thing done: breath called from the four winds into the slain, who stand up. In the vision the prophet has to speak the summons himself.

The reading asks in pairs: weak, make us strong; ignorant, knowing; dead, alive. One of the oldest Upanishads gives a sacrificer three such lines to recite, out of the unreal, out of darkness, out of death. A child’s prayer later in the guide runs the same way.

Three readings long for reunion and beg not to be left far off. Rūmī opens his great poem with that longing, given to a reed cut from its bed: all its music is complaint of separation and desire for the day of return.

The readings ask to be drawn near and brought to the meeting. In a saying the Prophet reports as God’s own words, each approach is answered with more than was given: a span is met by a cubit, and walking by running.

Seneca writes to a friend that no journey toward God is needed and no keeper of a temple need be begged: God is already within. Two readings ask to be brought to a presence and a meeting. Is the distance they speak of one that Seneca has overlooked, or one he denies?

The reading asks for a rain that will cleanse hearts of whatever keeps them from beholding God’s face. The penitent of Psalm 51 asks the same for one heart, his own, and fears the same loss: to be cast away from the presence.

The Buddha’s verse denies what the reading asks: no one can purify another. The reading prays that hearts be cleansed from above, and another asks God to “enable us to conquer self”. Who does the cleansing when the one who prays for it also sets to work?

The reading asks where the light of guidance is while people are in “the abyss of perdition and error”, and asks it of God. Arnold, hearing the tide go out at Dover, hears faith itself withdrawing, and turns to the one person beside him. The reading’s question is still a prayer; his poem has stopped addressing God.

The reading asks for a rain from the clouds of mercy that will cleanse the earth of “every transgressor”. Jesus speaks of a rain that falls on the just and the unjust alike, and bids his hearers pray for their persecutors, as two later readings do. Can one prayer ask both?

The reading is a prayer written for a child to say: “I am a little babe.” The best-known child’s prayer in English, first printed, as far as is known, in a New England schoolbook, is four lines for bedtime, and asks that the soul be kept. Both give a child words about another world before the child can weigh them.

The child of the reading asks to be made heavenly, illumined, spiritual, as though starting from earth. Wordsworth has the child arrive from God with heaven still about it, and lose the light in growing up. Is the prayer asking for something new, or for something to be kept?

The reading asks that a servant’s “entire being be dedicated to Thy service”. Ignatius gives those who make his Exercises the words for that dedication, faculty by faculty, with one request at the end: love and grace, “for this is enough for me”.

Two readings ask that deeds be made worthy of acceptance, “adorned with the ornament of Thy good-pleasure”. The Psalmist asks it of his words and of the thoughts behind them, in the last line of a psalm about the heavens and the law.
What the two readings ask, that deeds be made pleasing, Herbert asks by another road: to see God in every task and to do it “as for Thee”. Then, he says, even sweeping a room is adorned.

Huck kneels to ask help to do what he has been taught is right, and the words will not come while part of him means otherwise. The reading asks for aid “in that which Thou lovest”. What Huck had been taught to call right was betraying a runaway slave: his heart was sounder than his prayer.

Three readings ask God to aid his servants to do what he loves. Augustine’s sentence goes a step further: let God give the very thing he commands. Pelagius, hearing it quoted, objected that it left the human will nothing to do.

The reading asks for help to love God and gain his good-pleasure. Krishna tells Arjuna how every act can be turned that way: eating, giving, praying, fasting, all done as an offering. The reading asks for the love; the Gītā describes the practice.

The reading is a prayer in a woman’s voice: “I am she, O my God, who has turned toward the seat of the throne of Thy mercy.” The Bible’s fullest picture of a person praying alone and in silence is also of a woman, Hannah; the priest on duty took her for drunk.

quran-good-in-both-worlds.text: Our Lord! Give unto us in the world that which is good and in the Hereafter that which is good, and guard us from the doom of Fire.

quran-best-of-inheritors.text: And Zachariah, when he cried unto his Lord: My Lord! Leave me not childless, though Thou art the Best of inheritors.

psalm-forsaken.text: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring? O my God, I cry in the day time, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent.

quran-moses-loose-knot.text: (Moses) said: My Lord! relieve my mind And ease my task for me; And loose a knot from my tongue, That they may understand my saying.

matthew-daily-bread.text: Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.

shakespeare-beg-our-harms.text: We, ignorant of ourselves, / Beg often our own harms, which the wise powers / Deny us for our good; so find we profit / By losing of our prayers.
shakespeare-beg-our-harms.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

aesop-hercules-waggoner.text: "O Hercules, help me in this my hour of distress," quoth he. But Hercules appeared to him, and said: "Tut, man, don't sprawl there. Get up and put your shoulder to the wheel." The gods help them that help themselves.
aesop-hercules-waggoner.author: Aesop

hadith-anxiety-debt.text: O Allah! I seek refuge with You from worry and grief, from incapacity and laziness, from cowardice and miserliness, from being heavily in debt and from being overpowered by (other) men.
hadith-anxiety-debt.author: Muḥammad
hadith-anxiety-debt.caveat: The word in brackets is the translator’s.

julian-ground-of-beseeching.text: I am Ground of thy beseeching: first it is my will that thou have it; and after, I make thee to will it; and after, I make thee to beseech it and thou beseechest it. How should it then be that thou shouldst not have thy beseeching?
julian-ground-of-beseeching.author: Julian of Norwich

analects-praying-long.text: The Master being very sick, Tsze-lu asked leave to pray for him. He said, "May such a thing be done?" Tsze-lu replied, "It may. In the Eulogies it is said, 'Prayer has been made for thee to the spirits of the upper and lower worlds.'" The Master said, "My praying has been for a long time."
analects-praying-long.author: Confucius

rigveda-gayatri.text: May we attain that excellent glory of Savitar the God: So may he stimulate our prayers.

quran-way-out.text: And whosoever keepeth his duty to Allah, Allah will appoint a way out for him, And will provide for him from (a quarter) whence he hath no expectation. And whosoever putteth his trust in Allah, He will suffice him.

matthew-heavy-laden.text: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

marcus-turn-thy-prayers.text: Another prays thus: How shall I be released from this? Pray thou: How shall I not desire to be released? Another thus: How shall I not lose my little son? Thou thus: How shall I not be afraid to lose him? In fine, turn thy prayers this way, and see what comes.
marcus-turn-thy-prayers.author: Marcus Aurelius

matthew-cup-pass.text: And he went a little farther, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.

lovelace-stone-walls.text: Stone walls do not a prison make, / Nor iron bars a cage; / Minds innocent and quiet take / That for an hermitage; / If I have freedom in my love / And in my soul am free, / Angels alone, that soar above, / Enjoy such liberty.
lovelace-stone-walls.author: Richard Lovelace

johnson-leave-to-heaven.text: Still raise for Good the supplicating Voice, / But leave to Heav'n the Measure and the Choice. / Safe in his Pow'r, whose Eyes discern afar / The secret Ambush of a specious Pray'r. / Implore his Aid, in his Decisions rest, / Secure whate'er he gives, he gives the best.
johnson-leave-to-heaven.author: Samuel Johnson

quran-thou-knowest.text: Thou knowest what is in my mind, and I know not what is in Thy Mind. Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Knower of Things Hidden?

paine-change-his-mind.text: He prays dictatorially. When it is sunshine, he prays for rain, and when it is rain, he prays for sunshine. He follows the same idea in everything that he prays for; for what is the amount of all his prayers, but an attempt to make the Almighty change his mind, and act otherwise than he does? It is as if he were to say—thou knowest not so well as I.
paine-change-his-mind.author: Thomas Paine

buddha-lamps-unto-yourselves.text: Therefore, O Ananda, be ye lamps unto yourselves. Be ye a refuge to yourselves. Betake yourselves to no external refuge. Hold fast to the truth as a lamp. Hold fast as a refuge to the truth. Look not for refuge to any one besides yourselves.
buddha-lamps-unto-yourselves.author: The Buddha
buddha-lamps-unto-yourselves.work: Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (The Book of the Great Decease)
buddha-lamps-unto-yourselves.year: c. 5th century BCE; written down later
buddha-lamps-unto-yourselves.caveat: Copied from a scanned book, so the accent on Ânanda is missing.

saadi-every-breath.text: Every inhalation of the breath prolongs life and every expiration of it gladdens our nature; wherefore every breath confers two benefits and for every benefit gratitude is due. Whose hand and tongue is capable To fulfil the obligations of thanks to him?
saadi-every-breath.author: Saʿdī

numbers-priestly-blessing.text: The Lord bless thee, and keep thee: The Lord make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The Lord lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.

tennyson-wrought-by-prayer.text: More things are wrought by prayer / Than this world dreams of. Wherefore, let thy voice / Rise like a fountain for me night and day. / For what are men better than sheep or goats / That nourish a blind life within the brain, / If, knowing God, they lift not hands of prayer / Both for themselves and those who call them friend? / For so the whole round earth is every way / Bound by gold chains about the feet of God.
tennyson-wrought-by-prayer.author: Alfred Tennyson

chronicles-thine-is-the-kingdom.text: Thine, O Lord is the greatness, and the power, and the glory, and the victory, and the majesty: for all that is in the heaven and in the earth is thine; thine is the kingdom, O Lord, and thou art exalted as head above all.

tao-name-that-can-be-named.text: The Tâo that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tâo. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name.
tao-name-that-can-be-named.author: Laozi
tao-name-that-can-be-named.caveat: Copied from a scanned book, in which the printed Tâo was misread; it is restored here.

matthew-vain-repetitions.text: But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking. Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him.

quran-blessings-on-prophet.text: Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation.

tagore-leave-this-chanting.text: Leave this chanting and singing and telling of beads! Whom dost thou worship in this lonely dark corner of a temple with doors all shut? Open thine eyes and see thy God is not before thee! He is there where the tiller is tilling the hard ground and where the path-maker is breaking stones. He is with them in sun and in shower, and his garment is covered with dust.
tagore-leave-this-chanting.author: Rabindranath Tagore
tagore-leave-this-chanting.caveat: Tagore’s own English version of his Bengali poem.

quran-night-of-power.text: Lo! We revealed it on the Night of Predestination. Ah, what will convey unto thee what the Night of Power is! The Night of Power is better than a thousand months. The angels and the Spirit descend therein, by the permission of their Lord, with all decrees. (The night is) Peace until the rising of the dawn.

wesley-strangely-warmed.text: About a quarter before nine, while he was describing the change which God works in the heart through faith in Christ, I felt my heart strangely warmed. I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation; and an assurance was given me that He had taken away my sins, even mine, and saved me from the law of sin and death.
wesley-strangely-warmed.author: John Wesley

hopkins-send-my-roots-rain.text: See, banks and brakes / Now, leavèd how thick! lacèd they are again / With fretty chervil, look, and fresh wind shakes / Them; birds build—but not I build; no, but strain, / Time's eunuch, and not breed one work that wakes. / Mine, O thou lord of life, send my roots rain.
hopkins-send-my-roots-rain.author: Gerard Manley Hopkins

shelley-west-wind.text: Make me thy lyre, even as the forest is: / What if my leaves are falling like its own! / The tumult of thy mighty harmonies / Will take from both a deep, autumnal tone, / Sweet though in sadness. Be thou, spirit fierce, / My spirit! Be thou me, impetuous one! / Drive my dead thoughts over the universe / Like withered leaves to quicken a new birth!
shelley-west-wind.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley

ezekiel-breath.text: Then said he unto me, Prophesy unto the wind, prophesy, son of man, and say to the wind, Thus saith the Lord God; Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live. So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up upon their feet, an exceeding great army.

rumi-reed.text: Hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains, / Lamenting its banishment from its home: / "Ever since they tore me from my osier bed, / My plaintive notes have moved men and women to tears. / I burst my breast, striving to give vent to sighs, / And to express the pangs of my yearning for my home. / He who abides far away from his home / Is ever longing for the day he shall return.
rumi-reed.author: Jalāl al-Dīn Rūmī

hadith-draw-near.text: if he comes one span nearer to Me, I go one cubit nearer to him; and if he comes one cubit nearer to Me, I go a distance of two outstretched arms nearer to him; and if he comes to Me walking, I go to him running.
hadith-draw-near.author: Muḥammad

rights.note: Modern translation (translator d. 2021); part of one sentence.

hadith-draw-near.caveat: The Prophet gives these as God’s words; such a saying is called a ḥadīth qudsī and is not part of the Qur’an.

seneca-god-is-near.text: We do not need to uplift our hands towards heaven, or to beg the keeper of a temple to let us approach his idol’s ear, as if in this way our prayers were more likely to be heard. God is near you, he is with you, he is within you.
seneca-god-is-near.author: Seneca

rights.note: Published in the United States in 1917; translator d. 1969. Two sentences.

psalm-clean-heart.text: Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me. Cast me not away from thy presence; and take not thy holy spirit from me. Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free spirit.

dhammapada-purify-oneself.text: By oneself the evil is done, by oneself one suffers; by oneself evil is left undone, by oneself one is purified. Purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another.

arnold-sea-of-faith.text: The sea of faith / Was once, too, at the full, and round earth's shore / Lay like the folds of a bright girdle furled. / But now I only hear / Its melancholy, long, withdrawing roar, / Retreating, to the breath / Of the night-wind, down the vast edges drear / And naked shingles of the world.
arnold-sea-of-faith.author: Matthew Arnold

brihadaranyaka-lead-me.text: Lead me from the unreal to the real! Lead me from darkness to light! Lead me from death to immortality!
brihadaranyaka-lead-me.caveat: Copied from a scanned book, where a footnote and a page heading stand between the second and third lines.

matthew-pray-for-persecutors.text: But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you; That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.

primer-now-i-lay-me.text: Now I lay me down to take my sleep / I pray the Lord my soul to keep, / If I should die before I wake, / I pray the Lord my soul to take.
primer-now-i-lay-me.locator: edition of 1737, as reprinted by Paul Leicester Ford (1897)
primer-now-i-lay-me.caveat: Copied from a scanned book. Later editions have the familiar first line, “Now I lay me down to sleep”.

wordsworth-clouds-of-glory.text: Our birth is but a sleep and a forgetting: / The Soul that rises with us, our life's Star, / Hath had elsewhere it's setting, / And cometh from afar: / Not in entire forgetfulness, / And not in utter nakedness, / But trailing clouds of glory do we come / From God, who is our home: / Heaven lies about us in our infancy!
wordsworth-clouds-of-glory.author: William Wordsworth
wordsworth-clouds-of-glory.work: Ode: Intimations of Immortality from Recollections of Early Childhood

ignatius-take-and-receive.text: Take, Lord, and receive all my liberty, my memory, my intellect, and all my will — all that I have and possess. Thou gavest it to me: to Thee, Lord, I return it! All is Thine, dispose of it according to all Thy will. Give me Thy love and grace, for this is enough for me.
ignatius-take-and-receive.author: Ignatius of Loyola

psalm-acceptable.text: Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O Lord, my strength, and my redeemer.

herbert-elixir.text: Teach me, my God and King, / In all things Thee to see, / And what I do in anything / To do it as for Thee: … A servant with this clause / Makes drudgery divine; / Who sweeps a room as for Thy laws, / Makes that and th' actions fine.
herbert-elixir.author: George Herbert

twain-pray-a-lie.text: I knowed very well why they wouldn't come. It was because my heart warn't right; it was because I warn't square; it was because I was playing double. I was letting on to give up sin, but away inside of me I was holding on to the biggest one of all. … deep down in me I knowed it was a lie—and He knowed it. You can't pray a lie—I found that out.
twain-pray-a-lie.author: Mark Twain

augustine-give-what-you-command.text: And my whole hope is only in Your exceeding great mercy. Give what You command, and command what You will.
augustine-give-what-you-command.author: Augustine of Hippo
augustine-give-what-you-command.caveat: New Advent prints this translation with “Thou” changed to “You”.

gita-all-as-offering.text: Whate'er thou doest, Prince! / Eating or sacrificing, giving gifts, / Praying or fasting, let it all be done / For Me, as Mine.
gita-all-as-offering.locator: 9.27, in Edwin Arnold’s verse (The Song Celestial)

samuel-hannah.text: Now Hannah, she spake in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard: therefore Eli thought she had been drunken. And Eli said unto her, How long wilt thou be drunken? put away thy wine from thee. And Hannah answered and said, No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the Lord.
